- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.5) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >78), model often overshoots and fails to correct — apply a “cool-down” rule: cap forecast increase after spike by 2–3% per day.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 70), model overreacts — adjust forecast to align with recent low mean, not trend.
- When sentiment is high (≥0.8) and model is flat or rising slowly, model underestimates volatility — increase forecast volatility or add 1–2% upward bias.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture late-period reversals — add a “tail correction”: if last 3 days of true outcome show downward trend, reduce final 3 forecast points by 1–2%.
- If sentiment history shows alternating highs/lows (e.g., 0.8, 0.0, 0.8), model tends to overfit recent sentiment — use sentiment smoothing (e.g., average last 3 sentiment values) to avoid overreaction.
